paragraphs: The last paper showed that the political saying examined there does not require the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments to be wholly unconnected with each other. Now I shall undertake to show something more. Unless these departments are connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional control over the others, the degree of separation that the maxim requires as essential to a free government can never in practice be properly maintained.

Everyone agrees that the powers properly belonging to one department ought not to be directly and completely administered by either of the others. It is equally clear that none of them ought to have, directly or indirectly, an overruling influence over the others in administering their respective powers. No one will deny that power is encroaching by nature and that it ought to be effectively held back from passing the limits assigned to it. Once we have distinguished in theory the several classes of power, according to whether their nature is legislative, executive, or judiciary, the next and hardest task is to provide some practical security for each against invasion by the others. What this security ought to be is the great problem to be solved.

Is it enough to mark the boundaries of these departments precisely in the constitution of the government, and to trust these parchment barriers against the encroaching spirit of power? The framers of most of the American constitutions appear to have relied chiefly on this security. But experience assures us that the effectiveness of the provision has been greatly overrated, and that the weaker members of the government indispensably need some more adequate defense against the stronger. The legislative department is everywhere extending the sphere of its activity and drawing all power into its impetuous vortex.

The founders of our republics deserve so much credit for their wisdom that no task could be less pleasing than pointing out the errors they have fallen into. Respect for truth, however, requires us to remark that they seem never for a moment to have taken their eyes off one danger to liberty: the overgrown and all-grasping prerogative of a hereditary monarch, supported and fortified by a hereditary branch of the legislative authority. They seem never to have remembered the danger from legislative usurpations. These, by gathering all power into the same hands, must lead to the same tyranny that executive usurpations threaten.

In a government where an hereditary monarch holds numerous and extensive prerogatives, the executive department is very justly regarded as the source of danger, and is watched with all the jealousy that zeal for liberty ought to inspire. In a democracy, a multitude of people exercise the legislative functions in person. Because they cannot deliberate regularly or act in concert, they are continually exposed to the ambitious intrigues of their chief executives, and tyranny may well be feared to spring up in that same quarter on some favorable occasion. But take a representative republic. There the executive office is carefully limited in both the extent and the duration of its power. The legislative power is exercised by an assembly which, from a supposed influence over the people, is filled with fearless confidence in its own strength. That assembly is numerous enough to feel all the passions that move a multitude, yet not so numerous as to be unable to pursue the objects of those passions by means that reason prescribes. It is against the enterprising ambition of this department that the people ought to turn all their jealousy and exhaust all their precautions.

The legislative department draws its superiority in our governments from other circumstances too. Its constitutional powers are at once more extensive and less capable of precise limits. It can therefore more easily mask, under complicated and indirect measures, the encroachments it makes on the coordinate departments. In legislative bodies it is often a question of real delicacy whether a particular measure's operation will or will not go beyond the legislative sphere. On the other side, the executive power is confined to a narrower compass and is simpler in nature, and the judiciary is marked out by landmarks still less uncertain. Any project of usurpation by either of these departments would therefore betray and defeat itself at once. Nor is this all. Only the legislative department has access to the pockets of the people. In some constitutions it has full discretion, and in all it has a prevailing influence, over the pay of those who fill the other departments. That creates a dependence in the other departments, and it gives the legislature still greater ease in encroaching on them.

I have appealed to our own experience for the truth of what I say on this subject. If this experience needed to be confirmed with particular proofs, they could be multiplied without end. I could find a witness in every citizen who has taken part in the course of public administrations, or paid attention to it. I could gather abundant testimony from the records and archives of every State in the Union. But I will offer evidence that is shorter and just as satisfactory: the example of two States, vouched for by two unexceptionable authorities.

The first example is Virginia, a State which, as we have seen, has expressly declared in its constitution that the three great departments ought not to be intermixed. The authority in support of it is Mr. Jefferson. Besides his other advantages for observing how the government works, he was himself its chief executive. To convey fully the ideas his experience gave him on this subject, I must quote a passage of some length from his very interesting Notes on the State of Virginia, p. 195. "All the powers of government, legislative, executive, and judiciary, result to the legislative body. The concentrating these in the same hands, is precisely the definition of despotic government. It will be no alleviation, that these powers will be exercised by a plurality of hands, and not by a single one. One hundred and seventy-three despots would surely be as oppressive as one. Let those who doubt it, turn their eyes on the republic of Venice. As little will it avail us, that they are chosen by ourselves. An ELECTIVE DESPOTISM was not the government we fought for; but one which should not only be founded on free principles, but in which the powers of government should be so divided and balanced among several bodies of magistracy, as that no one could transcend their legal limits, without being effectually checked and restrained by the others. For this reason, that convention which passed the ordinance of government, laid its foundation on this basis, that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct, so that no person should exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time. BUT NO BARRIER WAS PROVIDED BETWEEN THESE SEVERAL POWERS. The judiciary and the executive members were left dependent on the legislative for their subsistence in office, and some of them for their continuance in it. If, therefore, the legislature assumes executive and judiciary powers, no opposition is likely to be made; nor, if made, can be effectual; because in that case they may put their proceedings into the form of acts of Assembly, which will render them obligatory on the other branches. They have accordingly, IN MANY instances, DECIDED RIGHTS which should have been left to JUDICIARY CONTROVERSY, and THE DIRECTION OF THE EXECUTIVE, DURING THE WHOLE TIME OF THEIR SESSION, IS BECOMING HABITUAL AND FAMILIAR."

The other State I shall use as an example is Pennsylvania, and the other authority is the Council of Censors, which met in 1783 and 1784. Part of this body's duty, as the constitution laid it out, was "to inquire whether the constitution had been preserved inviolate in every part; and whether the legislative and executive branches of government had performed their duty as guardians of the people, or assumed to themselves, or exercised, other or greater powers than they are entitled to by the constitution." In carrying out this trust, the council had necessarily to compare the proceedings of both the legislature and the executive with these departments' constitutional powers. The facts the council set out were mostly accepted as true by both sides in it. They show that the legislature had flagrantly violated the constitution in a variety of important instances.

A great many laws had been passed in violation of the rule that all bills of a public nature must first be printed for the people's consideration, and no apparent necessity excused the violation. Yet this is one of the precautions the constitution chiefly relies on against improper acts of the legislature.
The constitutional right to trial by jury had been violated, and powers had been taken that the constitution had not delegated.

The salaries of the judges, which the constitution expressly requires to be fixed, had at times been changed, and cases belonging to the judiciary department had often been pulled into legislative hearing and decision.

Anyone who wants to see the particulars under each of these heads may consult the council's journals, which are in print. It will be found that some of them may be blamed on peculiar circumstances connected with the war, but that most may be regarded as the spontaneous offshoots of an ill-constituted government.

It appears, also, that the executive department had not been innocent of frequent breaches of the constitution. Three observations ought to be made on this head, however. FIRST, a great proportion of the cases were either produced directly by the necessities of the war, or recommended by Congress or the commander-in-chief. SECOND, in most of the other cases, they conformed to the declared or known views of the legislative department. THIRD, the executive department of Pennsylvania differs from that of the other States in the number of members that make it up. In this respect it is as much like a legislative assembly as like an executive council. It is exempt at once from the restraint of individual responsibility for the acts of the body, and it draws confidence from mutual example and joint influence. Unauthorized measures would therefore, of course, be ventured more freely than where the executive department is administered by a single hand, or by a few hands.

The conclusion I am warranted in drawing from these observations is that merely marking the constitutional limits of the several departments on parchment is not a sufficient guard against those encroachments which lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.
